title: Exposed feedback and sign-in credentials
summary: An anonymous client could read 100 production feedback records. Separately, I saw sign-in codes reach analytics providers and saw one test session receive the other’s credentials after approval.

findings.name: Anonymous access to 100 production feedback records
findings.evidence: The 100 records contained feedback text, device details and account identifiers for 97 distinct usernames. I could read the sample without a member sign-in.

findings.name: Sign-in codes sent to three analytics providers
findings.evidence: I observed sign-in codes in outgoing analytics events for three third parties. That capture established that the codes left the service. Whether any recipient retained or redeemed a code remains unknown.

findings.name: A separate session received my account credentials after approval
findings.evidence: I controlled both sessions. After I approved sign-in with my test account, the other session received that account’s access and refresh credentials. The recorded test ends at credential delivery. An account takeover would require the account holder’s interaction.

research.title: Approval and credential delivery
research.adaptation: I recorded which session approved the sign-in and which session received the credentials. Keeping the two roles separate let me follow what happened after the user’s approval.
research.result: The second session received both access and refresh credentials for the approving account. My evidence ends at credential delivery.

research.title: Push notifications · background reading

papers.title: The Medium is the Message: How Secure Messaging Apps Leak Sensitive Data to Push Notification Services
papers.approach: The authors examined what Android messaging apps send through a push provider, including whether notification payloads reveal message content.

research.adaptation: My messaging notes cite this paper as background. I checked whether a device that successfully registered for messaging would actually receive a notification.
research.result: Registration succeeded. No notification reached my test device. That left interception unproven. The feedback and sign-in findings came from separate observations.

decision: I recommended restricting feedback reads to the roles that need them, removing sign-in secrets from analytics events and making the receiving session clear to the person approving sign-in.

title: Tenant access to internal service-account password hashes
summary: I assessed a staging tenant at both the application and database layers. The application restricted the resource requests I checked. The database role granted to the same tenant exposed internal service-account password hashes.

findings.name: A staging tenant could read internal service-account password hashes
findings.evidence: My tenant role could read stored password verifiers belonging to internal service accounts. Exposure puts those accounts at risk of offline password guessing. Password recovery, use of an internal role and access to another tenant were outside the demonstrated impact.

findings.name: A tenant could read internal infrastructure settings
findings.evidence: I could read operational settings that described the service’s infrastructure. Separately, database privilege records showed write grants on internal operational tables. My test established the grants and made no changes to the tables.

findings.name: Two staging sign-in flows enforced different anti-automation checks
findings.evidence: One flow challenged the browser. Another issued a staging session for my own valid credentials without that challenge. The production service recognized the flow, but session issuance was verified only in staging.

research.title: One tenant, two permission boundaries
research.adaptation: I kept the tenant identity fixed. At the application layer I compared how the service handled unavailable resources. At the database layer I checked what that tenant role could actually read.
research.result: An inaccessible resource and a nonexistent one produced the same application response. The database independently returned internal service-account verifiers. The assessment used one tenant, so cross-tenant access remains an open question.

decision: I recommended narrowing the privileges inherited by tenant roles and reviewing the affected service credentials.

title: Internal API documentation and credentials in a mobile release
summary: I distinguished what the service would show a recognized application from what it would show a signed-in member. The clearest disclosure was an internal specification covering 44 endpoints.

findings.name: A documented client identifier exposed a 44-endpoint internal specification
findings.evidence: I compared missing, invalid and recognized client identities. An identifier found in published documentation opened the internal specification and reference metadata. Member-only operations still required an authorized session.

findings.name: Reusable application credentials shipped in a mobile release
findings.evidence: I found application credentials in the distributed client. Anyone with that release could obtain them. The credential finding and the 44-endpoint disclosure involved different identifiers. I did not establish member-level access with the credentials from the release.

research.title: Autocomplete · paper cited on a separate lead

papers.title: Seasonality Based Reranking of E-commerce Autocomplete Using Natural Language Queries
papers.approach: The authors trained a reranker to favor suggestions relevant to the time of year and evaluated the quality of the rankings.

research.adaptation: I cited this paper in my autocomplete notes. I examined the fields returned in suggestions and compared them with public profiles. My measure was which information became visible in bulk. I did not train or evaluate a ranking model.
research.result: Suggestions exposed semi-public profile metadata in bulk. I found no evidence of access to private member records through autocomplete and held that lead back. The internal specification and mobile credentials were separate findings.

decision: I prepared five reports from 13 leads. I recommended checking permissions on each operation and reviewing which credentials are distributed in public builds.

title: Identity-verification fields in ordinary profile responses
summary: A demo-associated account could read identity-verification fields in 49 of 50 sampled profiles. The field exposure was measurable. The severity depends on whether the records represented real people and what the demo account was intended to see.

findings.name: Identity-verification fields visible on 49 of 50 sampled profiles
findings.evidence: The detailed response returned fields for legal name, age, country and verification date. In a separate comparison, one view returned email addresses that another view omitted for the same caller. The records’ origin and the caller’s intended relationship to those profiles were unresolved.

findings.name: A working account could be created without an invitation
findings.evidence: I obtained a working, demo-associated account without supplying an invitation. The product also offered invite-based onboarding. The security impact depends on whether open signup was intentional and which records the new account was meant to see.

research.title: Field-by-field privacy check
research.adaptation: With the caller held fixed, I compared individual fields across profile views. Then I counted how many detailed responses contained verification data.
research.result: The two views disclosed different fields to the same caller. The 49-of-50 count measures field visibility in my sample. Determining whether this exposed real customer data requires verifying the records’ origin.

decision: I recommended confirming the origin of the records, then applying one field policy based on the caller’s role and relationship to the profile. Separately owned test workspaces would allow an ownership retest.

title: Browser trust, app registration and account isolation
summary: I evaluated what another web origin was allowed to request, who could register a client application and which account data remained restricted. Each question required its own evidence.

findings.name: Seven hosts reflected an untrusted web origin on sign-in redirects
findings.evidence: I recorded seven hosts reflecting an untrusted origin and advertising credential support. My captures were sign-in redirects. They established the policy behavior. A browser reading a signed-in user’s private response remained an unverified impact.

findings.name: An OAuth client could register without administrator review
findings.evidence: The service accepted my test application. Six follow-up attempts still required sign-in and multifactor authentication. The severity depended on the intended registration policy. The score and vector in my notes disagreed, so the rating remains provisional.

findings.name: Sign-in method metadata was visible before login
findings.evidence: The service returned authentication-method information before sign-in. A nonexistent address also received a response. A lookup result alone therefore could not establish whether a given person had an account.

research.title: Object ownership · papers cited in my test record

papers.title: Broken Object Level Authorization in the Wild: An Empirical Taxonomy from 100+ Bug Bounty Disclosures
papers.approach: The authors classified public reports by the ownership boundary at issue and the action allowed. They distinguished verified authorization failures from reports that only carried that label.

papers.title: AuthProbe: Specification-Driven, Multi-Identity Detection of Broken Object-Level Authorization in Recruitment API
papers.approach: AuthProbe compares access under multiple controlled identities and uses the true owner’s response as a reference.

research.adaptation: I cited the taxonomy and AuthProbe beside my ownership checks. I used an ownership comparison on individual API paths. My log distinguished my own resources from alternate identifiers, but did not include an independently verified owner for those identifiers or a run of the authors’ scanner.
research.result: Of 18 paths identified, two had a recorded pair of responses. My own resource was accessible in both pairs, and the alternate identifier returned 404 in each. Neither pair disclosed another user’s data. The other paths have no equivalent paired result.

research.title: Public tool descriptions · research context

papers.title: Exposed by Design: A Dynamic Security Assessment of Internet-Facing MCP Servers at Scale
papers.approach: The authors surveyed Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, then tested their behavior to distinguish exposed interfaces from unauthorized actions.

research.adaptation: My research plan cited this study. I narrowed the question to one service and checked whether a reader of its public tool catalog could use the tools.
research.result: The tool descriptions were public by design. My test did not complete authorization or execute a privileged tool. I revised the finding after confirming what the catalog was meant to expose.

decision: I recommended an explicit allowlist of trusted browser origins and a review of who can register applications. During the assessment I lowered eight preliminary severity ratings as the controls narrowed what I could demonstrate.
